sources: bioGraphic (science magazine), 'Snake Fake' (M. Pobis, photos M. Bowler, 2019): the sphinx hawk moth caterpillar Hemeroplanes triptolemus, photographed in Peru, is a snake mimic; when threatened it pulls air in through tiny holes in its surface and inflates its head into a triangular viper-like shape; its underside is patterned in faux snakeskin with eyespots that appear to glisten; if that fails it lunges as if to strike; it has no venom or actual weaponry; birds and lizards hunt it; experiments with artificial pastry-dough caterpillars found eyespots and a snake-shaped head improved survival against birds; sphinx moth caterpillars become fluffy moths; https://www.biographic.com/snake-fake/

Skelhorn J., Dorrington G., Hossie T.J., Sherratt T.N. (2014) 'The position of eyespots and thickened segments influence their protective value to caterpillars', Behavioral Ecology 25(6):1417-1422: naive chicks were most wary of artificial caterpillars with eyespots or a thickened section at the front end (like a head); the traits deter predators by making caterpillars resemble dangerous vertebrates, not just by being conspicuous; https://ideas.repec.org/a/oup/beheco/v25y2014i6p1417-1422..html

Area de Conservacion Guanacaste caterpillar database (D. H. Janzen and W. Hallwachs, University of Pennsylvania), voucher 91-SRNP-1284: Hemeroplanes triptolemus (Sphingidae) reared in Costa Rica, food plant Mandevilla subsagittata (Apocynaceae); https://junquillal.info/voucher/91-SRNP-1284

title: This Caterpillar Turns Itself Into a Fake Snake 🐍
tiktok_caption: this 'snake' is a caterpillar 🐍 it flips over, puffs up a fake viper head and even strikes. no venom at all. Would you pick it up? ✋ yes / 😱 no way #meatballmyths #learnontiktok #caterpillar #animalfacts

beats.say: This caterpillar can turn itself into a fake snake head. And it strikes.
So I shrank down to caterpillar size, to see the trick up close.
It's a hawkmoth caterpillar, from the rainforests of Central and South America.
Most of the time, it just munches leaves.
But bother it, and it pulls its head and legs in, and flips over.
Then it sucks air in through tiny holes, and puffs up into a viper head.
Two fake eyes stare at me. They even look wet and shiny.
A hungry bird or lizard sees a viper, and backs off.
Still not scared? It lunges, like it's going to bite.
Here's the twist. It has no venom. No fangs. Nothing.
The whole snake is a bluff. Made of air and paint.
And the bluff works. Scientists made fake caterpillars out of pastry dough.
The ones with eyespots and a snake-shaped head survived birds better.
In another test, chicks were most scared when the eyespots sat up front, where a head would be.
One day, it turns into a hawkmoth, a fluffy moth.
So if a tiny viper struck at you from a leaf, would you pick it up?
The scariest snake in the rainforest is a caterpillar full of air.
